title: NDVI Field Zones and Alerts from Drone Imagery
description:
Turns a multispectral drone orthomosaic into a field health map. The script computes NDVI = (NIR - Red) / (NIR + Red) per pixel with NumPy, splits the field into square zones (for example 10 m x 10 m) and reports for each zone the mean NDVI, the share of low pixels and a status: healthy, watch, stressed or critical.

  • Reads and writes GeoTIFF with tifffile, keeping the map coordinates, so zones can be exported as GeoJSON polygons and opened in QGIS or a farm management system.
  • Compares a flight with an earlier, co-registered flight and alerts when a zone's NDVI drops by more than a set amount.
  • Treats no-data pixels (outside the field, gaps in the mosaic) separately.

NDVI shows where vegetation is weaker, not why. Alerts therefore say "scout this zone": water stress, nutrient deficiency, disease and thin stands all lower NDVI.
implementationSteps: Fly the field with a multispectral camera that has red and near-infrared bands, with overlap and reflectance calibration as the camera vendor recommends.
Stitch the images into a reflectance orthomosaic GeoTIFF with OpenDroneMap, Pix4D or Agisoft Metashape.
Run python -m cropwatch with the red and NIR band numbers of your camera; the script computes NDVI and masks no-data pixels.
Choose the zone size (for example 10 m) to match how you can act in the field, such as sprayer or irrigation sections.
Set the NDVI class thresholds for your crop and growth stage; the defaults are for a closed canopy in mid season.
For change detection, pass an earlier flight on the same grid with --previous and set the drop alert threshold.
Open out/ndvi.tif and out/zones.geojson in QGIS or import them into your farm management system.
Scout the flagged zones and record what you find, so thresholds can be adjusted over the season.
performance:
Expectations, not measured results:

  • NDVI and zone statistics are vectorized NumPy operations: a mosaic of tens of millions of pixels is processed in seconds on a laptop; the limit is memory (about 4 bytes per pixel per band).
  • Goal: flag zones with weak or declining vegetation within hours after a flight, so scouting and irrigation can be planned the same day.
  • How well alerts match real problems depends on calibration and thresholds; check them against scouting notes from your own fields.
userExperience: After a flight the user runs one command and gets an NDVI GeoTIFF, a GeoJSON file with one polygon per zone (status, mean NDVI, change since the last flight) and a short JSON list of alerts. In QGIS or a farm app the zones show as a color-coded grid over the field.
